scope: Learning design and reference ownership only. Units are explanations or subsections, not a promised number of new pages; no assignment counts as publication, approval or adoption.

chapters.question: How can words carry a wallet seed?
chapters.scope: Keep entropy, checksum, seed derivation and the passphrase boundary together. Formosa and seed sharing are optional follow-ups with their own homes.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How can one seed produce a whole wallet?
chapters.scope: Keep chain codes, public derivation, hardened boundaries and the leaked-child warning. Derived application entropy belongs in a companion.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How does a wallet find the right branch?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP44/84/86 account, change and address branches and explain the recovery/discovery implication. Additional purposes and path notations belong in derivation-conventions.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How do several devices agree on the same wallet?
chapters.scope: Show why keys, order, paths, threshold and script type must agree. Contrast the derivation schemes, then show the BSMS setup exchange. Give the voting-pool variants short historical comparisons.
chapters.staticIllustration: Cosigners checking the same wallet recipe before producing one receive address.

chapters.question: How can a wallet describe all its receiving scripts?
chapters.scope: Keep BIP380–386 as the wallet recipe: script wrapper, key origin, derivation and checksum. Multipaths, tapscript threshold expressions and alternative containers belong in a companion.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: Can a spending policy be checked before anyone spends?
chapters.scope: Distinguish a policy, a structured Miniscript expression, a descriptor wrapper and the resulting Script. Show one signature-plus-time policy and what analysis can establish. Compare the earlier template proposal.
chapters.staticIllustration: Policy to typed fragments to Script to two possible satisfaction paths.

chapters.question: What should a signing device know about a wallet?
chapters.scope: Explain registering a compact, reviewable account policy on a constrained signer, then instantiating descriptors from a template and keys. Distinguish this account representation from a high-level Miniscript policy language and from chain-code delegation.
chapters.staticIllustration: A signer reviewing a descriptor template and key list before recognizing later addresses.

chapters.question: What must survive besides the seed?
chapters.scope: Follow the recovery task beyond the seed: descriptor/account metadata, labels, scan hints and saved timelock-recovery plans. Give each format its own payload and limitation. BIP138 public-key-derived backup encryption must not carry private keys; these formats do not collectively guarantee recovery.
chapters.staticIllustration: A recovery inventory showing the seed separately from wallet descriptions, labels, scan hints and recovery plans.

chapters.question: What does a different mnemonic presentation change?
chapters.scope: Explain Formosa sentence themes and BIP39 re-encoding as a Draft alternative representation. Identify which derivation boundary it shares and what the representation changes.
chapters.staticIllustration: Two word representations meeting at a labelled seed-derivation boundary.

chapters.question: How do wallets name and describe different derivation schemes?
chapters.scope: Explain purpose namespacing, nested-SegWit derivation and path templates after the existing path lesson. Give the closed dynamic-tree proposal a separate comparison row; a path notation is not a new key-derivation algorithm.
chapters.staticIllustration: Purpose and path-template labels over one key tree, with a separate dynamic-tree comparison.

chapters.question: What is being imported when a wallet accepts an encoded private key?
chapters.scope: Explain BIP38 encrypted individual private keys and the closed BIP178 WIF extension for intended script types. Keep both distinct from backing up a deterministic wallet seed and from recipient-address encoding.
chapters.staticIllustration: One private key passing through an import-format envelope or a passphrase-encryption envelope.

chapters.question: Can one root provide separate secrets for different applications?
chapters.scope: Explain BIP85 application-specific entropy from hardened BIP32 children and the root compromise boundary. Distinguish derived application entropy from another wallet account or an extra backup copy.
chapters.staticIllustration: One root with hardened branches ending in separately labelled application-entropy outputs.

chapters.question: How can a seed be checked or divided into recovery shares?
chapters.scope: Explain codex32 encoding, checksum and optional threshold shares. State what material recovery reconstructs and distinguish sharing a seed from requiring multiple signatures to spend.
chapters.staticIllustration: A seed and its checked encoding beside a threshold reconstruction of shares.

chapters.question: How can one descriptor express more branches or signing conditions?
chapters.scope: Build on the descriptor lesson with tapscript threshold expressions and receive/change multipaths. Give the closed binary-container proposal a comparison section; container encoding and script semantics are different changes.
chapters.staticIllustration: One descriptor expanding into two branches, alongside a tapscript threshold and a container comparison.

chapters.question: Which derivation information should each cosigner receive?
chapters.scope: Explain chain-code delegation and the coordinator/signer information boundary. State which derivations each party can perform and what a cosigner can still check; separate it from account-policy registration.
chapters.staticIllustration: Coordinator and signers separated by labelled key and chain-code information boundaries.

chapters.question: What does an address actually identify?
chapters.scope: Keep the Bech32/Bech32m encoding and validation lesson, including Bech32 for witness v0. Give address versus output-script context briefly; additional formats and private-key import formats have separate homes.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How can a script hide behind a hash?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP16 commitment, reveal and second script evaluation as one worked spend. Bare multisig and competing script-hash designs belong in the history reference.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: Why can valid signatures still need stricter rules?
chapters.scope: Separate DER encoding, signature malleability, NULLDUMMY, and deterministic low-r/low-s signing. Distinguish consensus rules, policy and a Draft signer algorithm; BIP147 is not an ECDSA equation change.
chapters.staticIllustration: Same payment intent passing through encoding, dummy-element and signer-choice checks.

chapters.question: What changes when signatures move into the witness?
chapters.scope: Keep transaction identity, witness separation, weight and BIP143 signing data. Peer serialization and mining-template fields are separate follow-ups.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: When is a coin allowed to move?
chapters.scope: Keep absolute and relative locks, sequence semantics and median-time-past together. Applications in recovery and contracts link back to this lesson.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How do wallets pass an unfinished transaction around?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP174 container and creator/updater/signer/finalizer workflow. Show why signers need context; v2, Taproot and specialized coordination fields belong in companions.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: What does a Schnorr signature prove?
chapters.scope: Keep one-signature verification, x-only keys and the BIP340 construction. Explain signature roles in place; detailed ECDSA encodings and MuSig2 are optional follow-ups.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: Why reveal only the spending path you use?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP341 key path, committed script tree, tweak and selective revelation. Historical MAST and alternative Merkle/execution designs belong in a separate reference.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How does a Taproot script get evaluated?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP342 execution and upgrade rules for a revealed Taproot script. Proposed operations and resource changes belong in the proposal path.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How can several people make one signature?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP327 n-of-n key aggregation and two signing rounds, including nonce discipline. Derivation, descriptor representation and PSBT transport belong in musig2-wallets.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How can a transaction get unstuck?
chapters.scope: Explain replacement, child-pays-for-parent, packages, pinning, restricted topology and keyless anchor outputs. Separate wallet strategy, mempool policy and peer messages; do not equate Draft status with absent implementations.
chapters.staticIllustration: A parent-child package with fee labels and a pinning versus replaceable topology comparison.

chapters.question: What can transaction shape reveal about a wallet?
chapters.scope: Compare deterministic ordering, mixed-input advice, anti-fee-sniping and the Draft dust-disposal convention. Present privacy rationales as claims with assumptions; do not recommend one universal sorting or disposal strategy.
chapters.staticIllustration: Four transaction silhouettes with labelled inference opportunities and limits.

chapters.question: What changes when you pay someone in bitcoin?
chapters.scope: Follow a symbolic payment from an unspent output through inputs, new outputs, change and a fee. Distinguish a wallet, a key, an address and a spending condition; introduce hashes and signatures only by their roles. Stop before serialization, derivation arithmetic and chain selection. Use public schematic values; this is a conceptual scaffold, not new BIP coverage.
chapters.staticIllustration: One payment storyboard: wallet selects an output, constructs a transaction, and proposes new recipient/change outputs.
chapters.sourceRequirement: Anchor the glossary to the existing evidence ledgers. Add pinned primary protocol documentation for UTXOs, change and fees; the listed BIPs alone are not a complete introductory source.

chapters.question: How do recipient encodings relate to output scripts?
chapters.scope: Compare Base58Check script-hash addresses with the existing witness-address lesson, explain the closed witness-address alternative and the recipient-identifier terminology proposal. Keep private-key import formats in private-key-backups.
chapters.staticIllustration: Each recipient string pointing to its output script, with proposed terminology labelled separately.

chapters.question: Which script-hash and multisig designs were compared with P2SH?
chapters.scope: Explain bare threshold multisig, then compare OP_EVAL, CHV, hashScriptCheck and the low-sigop multisig proposal by commitment, execution and resource rule. Do not insert this design history into the first P2SH spend.
chapters.staticIllustration: Bare multisig beside a compact alternative-design table.

chapters.question: How do PSBT construction and Taproot fields extend the same workflow?
chapters.scope: Compare v0 and v2 construction representation and show Taproot fields as a separate extension supported by both versions. Use BIP10 only as a short predecessor comparison. Specialized key tweaks, MuSig2 and Silent Payment workflows have separate homes.
chapters.staticIllustration: The same transaction folder with a v0/v2 representation axis and an independent Taproot-fields axis.

chapters.question: Which commitment and execution ideas preceded or differ from Taproot?
chapters.scope: Compare Fast Merkle Trees, the earlier MAST proposal, branch verification and tail calls. Give each its own mechanism and limit; do not imply Taproot implements these designs.
chapters.staticIllustration: Four labelled commitment/execution cards beside the already learned Taproot tree.

chapters.question: How does a MuSig2 signing group become a repeatable wallet?
chapters.scope: Connect aggregate-key derivation, musig() descriptors and PSBT coordination fields. Keep derivation and transport distinct from the signing algorithm. BIP373 fields work in both PSBT versions despite its header requirement.
chapters.staticIllustration: Participant keys to aggregate child key to descriptor, with nonce-round data in a separate PSBT lane.

chapters.question: How does a payment request reach a wallet?
chapters.scope: Explain bitcoin: instructions and their evolution, mandatory parameters, multiple payment methods and DNS discovery. Contrast alias resolution with BIP353; never imply DNSSEC authenticates the human recipient.
chapters.staticIllustration: Human-readable name to DNS instruction to URI to chosen payment method.

chapters.question: What did the merchant Payment Protocol add?
chapters.scope: Explain merchant requests, acknowledgements, MIME types, URI and HTTP negotiation, zero-value OP_RETURN and encrypted address exchange. Separate historical specification status from present wallet support.
chapters.staticIllustration: Merchant and payer exchanging request, transaction and acknowledgement, with trust and certificate labels.

chapters.question: Why would the receiver add an input to your payment?
chapters.scope: Explain the common-input heuristic, sender/receiver checks, synchronous negotiation, asynchronous directory delivery and the earlier Bustapay design. Payjoin changes construction, not consensus.
chapters.staticIllustration: Ordinary payment beside a collaboratively built transaction and a three-step directory mailbox flow.

chapters.question: Can one public payment code lead to fresh outputs?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP352 fresh-output derivation, sender/receiver work and scan tradeoff. Payment-code comparisons and signer/descriptor integration have separate homes.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: How can contract data determine a payment key?
chapters.scope: Separate two constructions. BIP175 hashes contract documents, sorts their hashes, hashes them with payment_base, maps the digest into non-hardened BIP32 path components, then derives a payment key/address. BIP372 carries generic pay-to-contract key-tweak information in PSBT for a signer. Do not draw BIP175 as a single additive key tweak or imply BIP372 directly implements its derivation path; neither is a covenant restricting future spends.
chapters.staticIllustration: Two labelled panels: contract documents → combined digest → child-index path → derived address; generic key tweak → PSBT signer information.

chapters.question: What can a wallet actually prove?
chapters.scope: Keep BIP322 message challenges and what a successful proof establishes. Other message, payment-history and reserve proof formats belong in a comparison reference.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: What can a hash and a deadline coordinate?
chapters.scope: Explain HTLC claim/refund paths and the collateral-contract application as uses of hashes and deadlines. State coordination and timeout assumptions without claiming complete Lightning coverage.
chapters.staticIllustration: Claim/refund paths on a shared timeline, then the collateral application.

chapters.question: What must a wallet coordinate to send and recover Silent Payments?
chapters.scope: Explain sp() descriptors and the distinct Silent Payment send/spend PSBT v2 workflows. Introduce DLEQ only when a signer must show that two public points share the same secret; the proof does not authorize spending. Leave MuSig2 nonce coordination to its own companion.
chapters.staticIllustration: Separate send and spend lanes, with ECDH shares/proofs and descriptor scan information labelled.

chapters.question: How do reusable payment codes trade notification against scanning?
chapters.scope: Compare BIP47 and BIP351 mechanisms with the existing Silent Payments explanation using notification, sender work, receiver work and information leakage. Record BIP63 only as an allocation; it has no published mechanism to teach.
chapters.staticIllustration: Notification and scanning flows with distinct information boundaries.

chapters.question: What claims do other wallet proof formats establish?
chapters.scope: Compare legacy compact message signatures, proof of a past payment and its URI exchange, and proof-of-reserves transactions with BIP322. Distinguish key control, payment history, funds availability and solvency.
chapters.staticIllustration: A table of claim, witness, verifier and what remains unproved.

chapters.question: How can locking coins make an identity costly to replace?
chapters.scope: Explain timelocked fidelity bonds and certificates as a proposed cost signal. State the observer and reuse assumptions; a cost signal is not a guarantee that its owner will behave honestly.
chapters.staticIllustration: Locked coins connected to a certificate and an observer judging the cost signal.

chapters.question: What changes when wallets display amounts or exchange rates differently?
chapters.scope: Compare denomination proposals and exchange-rate interfaces. Explain units, rate source and conversion assumptions separately; display conventions change no consensus amount.
chapters.staticIllustration: One underlying amount with alternative display units and a separate external exchange-rate source.

chapters.question: Does a reference name a transaction or a position in a chain?
chapters.scope: Explain blockchain URIs and transaction-position references, including network and confirmation context. A chain position is not the same identifier as a transaction hash.
chapters.staticIllustration: Transaction hash versus block/position locator, each with its network context.

chapters.question: How do two Bitcoin peers agree what they can do?
chapters.scope: Explain protocol version and user agent, liveness, modern feature negotiation, and the earlier custom-service proposal. Put proof-of-work connection challenges in a separate comparison box about resource admission.
chapters.staticIllustration: A short peer handshake with liveness and feature cards; a distinct challenge/solution admission sketch.

chapters.question: How do you find a peer that can serve you?
chapters.scope: Explain address gossip across network types and the limited historical service advertised by pruned peers. A service bit is a capability advertisement, not a trust guarantee.
chapters.staticIllustration: Address-book entries for different networks beside full-history and pruned-history service ranges.

chapters.question: Which announcements should a peer send?
chapters.scope: Explain mempool inventory requests, transaction relay flags, reject messages, header preference, fee filters and the closed no-transaction-relay proposal. Treat Deployed as source metadata, not a claim that modern nodes still expose every message.
chapters.staticIllustration: A peer message menu showing request, preference, rejection and filtering as different operations.

chapters.question: How can peers relay a block without resending everything?
chapters.scope: Explain compact-block short IDs, reconstruction and missing transactions. Contrast stale-tip announcements as fork-observation information rather than block compression or a new chain-selection rule.
chapters.staticIllustration: Known transactions filling compact-block slots, with a small stale-branch announcement inset.

chapters.question: How can peers avoid sending the same transaction twice?
chapters.scope: Start with witness-aware peer serialization and transaction identity. Then separate reconciliation of announcements from payload compression, flagging BIP337 lossy-outpoint limits. Each mechanism has its own section; these are alternative bandwidth boundaries, not one required upgrade package.
chapters.staticIllustration: Three layers: transaction identity/serialization, announcement-set reconciliation and optional payload compression.

chapters.question: What can a light wallet learn without a full node?
chapters.scope: Compare specialized-node roles, server-side Bloom matching and service opt-in, UTXO queries, and size/weight fraud proofs. Explain proof scope, omission risks and privacy before linking to client-side block filters.
chapters.staticIllustration: Who sends the query, who sees it, and what is actually proved across three light-client designs.

chapters.question: How can a wallet scan without giving a server its addresses?
chapters.scope: Keep BIP157/158 as one client/server protocol and encoding lesson, including matching, false positives and trust limits. Older server-side query schemes are an optional comparison.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: What does encrypting a peer connection protect?
chapters.scope: Keep BIP324 opportunistic transport encryption and its limits. Authentication and source-routing privacy belong in a comparison reference.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: Which privacy property does each network design try to protect?
chapters.scope: Compare older authenticated/encrypted-channel proposals and Dandelion transaction routing with BIP324. Separate confidentiality against passive observers, peer authentication and source anonymity; no one property supplies the others.
chapters.staticIllustration: Observer boundary diagram with separate channel, identity and routing rows.

chapters.question: Which old consensus edge cases still need cleanup?
chapters.scope: Separate transaction/internal-Merkle-node ambiguity from worst-case validation, timewarp and duplicate-transaction cleanup. Compare the narrow BIP53 proposal with the broader Complete BIP54 package; Complete does not mean activated.
chapters.staticIllustration: A Merkle leaf/internal-node ambiguity sketch and a four-item consensus-cleanup checklist.

chapters.question: How did competing proposals try to set block limits?
chapters.scope: Group fixed increases, scheduled growth, miner voting, feedback algorithms and temporary data restrictions. Give each BIP its own comparison row with its actual rule and Closed status; do not retell every debate or imply deployment.
chapters.staticIllustration: One family table of what sets the limit, when it changes, and which resources it counts.

chapters.question: What other transaction designs were proposed?
chapters.scope: Compare replay protection, coalescing inputs, flexible serialization and normalized IDs. Explain which problem each closed design addressed and how its mechanism differs from SegWit; do not claim a formal replacement relationship.
chapters.staticIllustration: Four before/after transaction cards with the field or identity rule each proposal changes.

chapters.question: What does publishing a BIP actually mean?
chapters.scope: Explain proposal ownership, modern workflow and layers; compare earlier process and committee proposals and fork taxonomy. Separate editorial publication, specification completion, adoption and consensus enforcement.
chapters.staticIllustration: BIP publication workflow beside a separate implementation/adoption path, with no automatic arrow between them.

chapters.question: How can a soft fork become an enforced rule?
chapters.scope: Keep the BIP9/BIP8 signaling, lock-in and activation state machines. Explain that signaling is not validation and document status is not activation; historical deployments and process details are optional references.
chapters.staticIllustration: Reuse the existing focused drawings; add only short links to related explanations.

chapters.question: Who chooses the block a miner hashes?
chapters.scope: Explain node-to-miner block templates, pooled-mining extensions, SegWit template fields, Stratum extension negotiation and version rolling. Keep BIP40/41 as allocated-only records; do not imply a published BIP specification or full Stratum V2 coverage.
chapters.staticIllustration: Node to pool to hashing worker, labelled with template decisions, negotiated fields and version-bit uses.

chapters.question: Why does Bitcoin need more than one test network?
chapters.scope: Compare permissionless testnet difficulty behavior and signed-block Signet coordination. Explain Testnet4 versus Draft Testnet5 and BIP54 rules without implying the latter are active on mainnet.
chapters.staticIllustration: Three network cards comparing genesis, block admission, difficulty behavior and purpose.

chapters.question: What would miners control in a drivechain?
chapters.scope: Separate hashrate-escrow withdrawals from blind merged mining. Explain the proposed mainchain changes, miner influence and user trust assumptions; neither publication nor the word blind establishes security.
chapters.staticIllustration: Two independent arrows: mainchain escrow/withdrawal and sidechain block-selection bids.

chapters.question: What would changing proof of work actually change?
chapters.scope: Use a short historical chapter on the closed optical/low-energy PoW proposal. Explain the changed work function, deployment implications and the distinction between the authors energy rationale and demonstrated network properties.
chapters.staticIllustration: Existing hashing pipeline beside the proposed work pipeline, with changed assumptions labelled.

chapters.question: How does a proposed payment become part of a shared history?
chapters.scope: Separate transaction relay and local mempool policy, full-node validation, miner block construction, proof of work and chain selection. Show a temporary competing tip and why a valid block and a preferred chain are different judgments. Introduce soft forks and signaling as context for the existing activation lesson. Stop before individual peer messages, mining APIs and historical incidents.
chapters.staticIllustration: Wallet to peer mempools to candidate blocks to independent validation, with two competing tips and a separate signaling lane.
chapters.sourceRequirement: Use existing activation evidence plus pinned primary documentation for validation and chain selection. Check the general model independently; historical BIP case studies do not supply the whole foundation.

chapters.question: What do historical validation failures and fixes teach us?
chapters.scope: Use duplicate transaction protection, coinbase height, subsidy arithmetic and the 2013 database-induced chain split as case studies after readers understand nodes and chain selection. Explain the real arithmetic fix behind BIP42 satire. These examples illustrate particular failures; they are not a general definition of consensus.
chapters.staticIllustration: Four cases, each showing the disagreeing condition, resulting risk and rule or implementation response.

chapters.question: How did different deployment plans use or depart from signaling?
chapters.scope: Compare buried deployments, SegWit and Taproot deployment plans and generalized voting. Label each proposal status and distinguish what the document specifies from independently sourced activation history. Keep BIP8/BIP9 mechanics in the existing lesson.
chapters.staticIllustration: A dated comparison of triggers, thresholds and enforcement, with proposed and observed events explicitly distinguished.

chapters.question: Can a coin restrict the transaction that spends it?
chapters.scope: Compare checking a template commitment, exposing a configurable transaction hash, and pushing a template hash for use by other operations. Explain exact commitment fields and limits before applications; all are proposals, not current rules.
chapters.staticIllustration: An output pointing to allowed future transaction shapes; a three-column commitment comparison.

chapters.question: Can a signature be reused for a different state?
chapters.scope: Contrast ANYPREVOUT with the TEMPLATEHASH/CHECKSIGFROMSTACK/INTERNALKEY package. Explain what each signature commits to and why reusable states help channel designs. BIP448 is a deployment package, not a fourth independent opcode.
chapters.staticIllustration: Two compatible transaction states sharing authorization, plus the three-opcode package stack.

chapters.question: Can a wallet give you time to stop a theft?
chapters.scope: Explain delayed withdrawal and recovery, then compare specialized OP_VAULT with more general contract-verification commitments. Keep BIP345 closed and its Proposed-Replacement relationship distinct from deployment or exact equivalence.
chapters.staticIllustration: Deposit to delayed withdrawal or emergency recovery, with contract-state commitments marked.

chapters.question: What can a few extra script operations unlock?
chapters.scope: Give concatenation, pair commitments and x-only key tweaking their own short sections. Explain their different primitives and composition limits, with explicit proposal statuses. A Complete BIP347 document does not mean OP_CAT is active.
chapters.staticIllustration: Three input/output stack cards, each showing precisely one new operation.

chapters.question: How much work should a script be allowed to do?
chapters.scope: Explain generalized operation budgets and the separate restoration proposal for a new tapleaf version. Connect cost and memory limits to denial-of-service resistance without presenting benchmark claims as universal guarantees.
chapters.staticIllustration: Opcode costs filling a budget meter beside the current and proposed script-resource boundaries.

chapters.question: What would a quantum-safe migration need?
chapters.scope: Separate removing the exposed Taproot key path from adding a post-quantum signature scheme and planning a legacy-signature sunset. Record BIP361 unresolved Requires text; do not invent a PQ-signature BIP or repeat the authors hardware forecasts as fact.
chapters.staticIllustration: Exposed key path versus committed script path, followed by a migration plan with an explicitly missing signature-scheme prerequisite.

audience: A technically curious reader who knows what a Bitcoin payment is but does not yet understand wallet internals, Script or peer protocols. No curve arithmetic or implementation experience is assumed for the core route.

coreStages.title: Follow a payment
coreStages.outcome: Distinguish the coin being spent, the new outputs, the spending condition and the wallet constructing the transaction.
coreStages.check: In the drawing, point to what is consumed, what is created and what an address describes.

coreStages.title: Find and recover the right keys
coreStages.outcome: Explain the different jobs of a mnemonic, seed, derived key and recipient address.
coreStages.check: Which of these is secret, which can be shared, and which describes where a payment should go?

coreStages.title: Authorize a spend
coreStages.outcome: Trace the commitment, signature and revealed data for a spend, and explain what each proposal changes.
coreStages.check: Compare a P2SH spend with a Taproot key-path or script-path spend: what is committed, revealed and checked?

coreStages.title: Describe a wallet and coordinate devices
coreStages.outcome: Connect derivation conventions to a wallet recipe, then separate that recipe from a transaction container and each signer’s role.
coreStages.check: Why can recovery need more than a seed, and which extra information belongs in a descriptor versus a PSBT?

coreStages.title: Understand relay, validation and upgrades
coreStages.outcome: Distinguish local relay policy, block validity, chain selection and activation rules.
coreStages.check: Could one peer decline a transaction while another accepts it, and why is a signaling bit not itself proof of validity?

optionalTracks.title: Back up and recover a wallet
optionalTracks.outcome: Identify the secret and non-secret material needed for a particular recovery plan; distinguish derivation, sharing and metadata.

optionalTracks.title: Coordinate multiple signers
optionalTracks.outcome: Trace shared wallet setup and signing while distinguishing script multisig from aggregate signatures.

optionalTracks.title: Request payments and reason about privacy
optionalTracks.outcome: Separate recipient discovery, transaction collaboration, fee policy, output privacy and proof of control.

optionalTracks.title: Build spending and recovery conditions
optionalTracks.outcome: Read a spending condition and state its authorization, timeout and resource assumptions.

optionalTracks.title: Follow data through the peer network
optionalTracks.outcome: Explain which data a peer sends, what a light client can verify and what transport encryption protects.

optionalTracks.title: Study consensus and mining
optionalTracks.outcome: Distinguish a validation rule, mining interface, deployment mechanism and test-network choice; evaluate proposed changes by their assumptions.

optionalTracks.title: Evaluate proposed script changes
optionalTracks.outcome: Compare proposed capabilities against the existing spending model without treating document status as activation.

deliveryBatches.title: Make the core route understandable
deliveryBatches.purpose: Fill the two conceptual gaps and connect the existing lessons into the core route.
deliveryBatches.acceptance: A reader can trace the same schematic payment from wallet construction to node validation and distinguish those roles. Review the two primer sources; preserve existing lesson scopes and figure IDs.

deliveryBatches.title: Complete one shared-wallet workflow
deliveryBatches.purpose: Connect descriptor/PSBT fundamentals to consistent multisig setup and version-aware signing.
deliveryBatches.acceptance: A static worked setup shows agreement on keys, order, paths and script type; a separate compatibility table correctly distinguishes PSBT version from Taproot fields.

deliveryBatches.title: Complete one payment-request workflow
deliveryBatches.purpose: Connect a payment request to a collaboratively built transaction and its privacy assumptions.
deliveryBatches.acceptance: A request-to-transaction storyboard identifies the recipient-discovery trust boundary and every sender/receiver check claimed by the explanation.
